title: James Gunn Says ‘No One From Skydance’ Has Seen ‘Superman’ Sequel ‘Man of Tomorrow’ as Rumors Fly After His DC Studios Exit
full_text: × Nov 14, 2026 7:27am PT James Gunn Says ‘No One From Skydance’ Has Seen ‘Superman’ Sequel ‘Man of Tomorrow’ as Rumors Fly After His DC Studios Exit By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest Gambit Gets Serious: Channing Tatum’s Superhero Is ‘Not All Laughs’ in ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ as Kevin Feige Promises Fans a ‘Fully-Rounded Character’ 17 hours ago Gal Gadot Says Skydance Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz ‘Gives Me Hope’ Against Antisemitism: ‘I’m Frightened by How Quickly Hatred of Jews Is Spreading’ 2 days ago Tarantino Fired Mélanie Laurent From ‘Inglourious Basterds’ After ‘Terrible’ Table Read and Axed Isabelle Huppert for Not Showing Up: ‘I Don’t Owe You Jack S—‘ 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection James Gunn took to Threads to clarify a rumor about his exit from DC Studios: It had nothing to do with the upcoming “ Superman ” sequel “ Man of Tomorrow ” worrying executives at Warner Bros.’ new parent company, Skydance . Rumors have circulated on social media alleging the film’s poor quality is one of the reasons Gunn got the boot after four years as co-CEO of DC Studios alongside Peter Safran. The rumors snowballed into claims Skydance would dump “Man of Tomorrow” onto streaming via HBO Max amid yet another DC Universe overhaul, this time under president and chief creative officer Jeremy Latcham. Related Stories What to Watch on Disney+ in November 2026 The Game Awards to Reveal 2026 Nominees Next Week Ahead of ‘GTA 6’ Debut, PlayStation 5 Joins Livestreamers for December Show (EXCLUSIVE) “There are a lot of untrue rumors going around, but one of them is that Skydance has seen ‘Man of Tomorrow’ and that all sorts of sweeping changes are being made,” Gunn posted on his Threads account denying the rumors. “No one from Skydance has even seen the movie – the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. So any stories around this narrative are false.” Gunn and Safran’s exits from DC Studios were announced Nov. 9. Their departures came as a shock considering the duo was named as part of Skydance’s business leadership team when Paramount’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery closed in October. Gunn and Safran became the heads of DC Studios in 2022 and their four-year stint included film releases like “Superman,” “Supergirl” and “Clayface” and television series like “Creature Commandos” and “Lanterns,” among others. Soon after the news broke, Gunn took to social media to express his feelings about the job and revealed that he had grown weary by the executive job. “What only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least,” Gunn wrote. “I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years” In his statement, Gunn also revealed that he’s “engaged on another DC project which I’m writing” in addition to post-production on “Man of Tomorrow.” The “Superman” sequel is currently on the release calendar for July 9, 2027. ‘Harry Potter’ HBO Series Casts Its Arthur Weasley, Moaning Myrtle, Colin Creevey ‘Harry Potter’ HBO Series Casts Sorting Hat, Nearly Headless Nick, and More Hogwarts Ghosts and Portraits ‘Harry Potter’ Star Paapa Essiedu Says ‘I Don’t Want to Talk About’ J.K. title: Why Bruce Buffer Traded the Octagon for the Steakhouse in New Bud Light Campaign
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All November 14, 2026 7:23am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bruce Buffer in the Bud Light "Chef" ad Bud Light As the UFC returns to Madison Square Garden Saturday night, UFC ring announcer Bruce Buffer is trading the octagon for a steakhouse in a new Bud Light spot. The campaign sees Buffer swap places with a steakhouse server so they can watch the big UFC fight, leaving him to serve the customers. Watch: “I love when I perform or even when I’m doing commercials to be self-deprecating,” Buffer tells The Hollywood Reporter about the spot. “I like making fun of myself and just having fun for comedy purposes, and the creative people at Bud Light, you know, when they send me the storyboards, I go, ‘This is going to be awesome.’ So I totally dug my teeth into it. I loved it.” Related Stories Movies Ben Stiller Gives Update on His New York Knicks Documentary: "The Pressure Is on" Business Why Jordan Brand Is Using a 'Space Jam' Docuseries to Launch "Jordan TV" The Bud Light spot was released ahead of UFC 334, which will take place tonight at Madison Square Garden in New York City. Bud Light is an official sponsor of UFC, with its spots typically running during the broadcast both for viewers and those in the arena. “Bud Light’s creative team is just really fantastic at what they do, and looking at that, I trust them to come up with what they came up with, and they also give me the freedom to give feedback,” says Buffer. “It’s really, really cool, and it’s great when you work with people that are that comfortable to work with and respect the fact that they’re not damaging your brand, but yet enhancing it.” In addition to the spot, Bud Light is partnering with UFC and Omaha Steaks on a “Fight Night Feast” package, which will bundle tomahawk steaks, Bud Light beer money, a Paramount+ gift card and UFC training gloves for $99. “We know the best part of fight night is getting together with friends over an ice-cold Bud Light and some great food,” said Todd Allen, senior VP of marketing for Bud Light at Anheuser-Busch. “And with UFC 335 set to close out the year, we wanted to create something for UFC fans that makes fight night easy to enjoy. Fight Night Feast delivers everything needed for an unforgettable night of UFC action directly to fans’ doorsteps.” But it’s also a testament to how far UFC has come. What was once an outcast sport now counts America’s biggest beer brand as a sponsor. “When I started with the UFC 30 years ago, we were a spectacle. We weren’t what I would consider a sport,” Buffer recalls. “It was like a blood sport, like the movie. It was what style is the best? It grew with the rules and became mixed martial arts seven or eight years into its evolutionary process, to now where it’s a mainstream sport, to where we’re accepted by the Paramount networks and all the other big networks of this world, and to get to the point now where we’re working with Bud Light and mainstream sponsors that work with the other major sports in the world, it shows that UFC is truly the biggest fighting event in the world and is a mainstream sport. It’s like we made it. It’s a clarification that we’re there.” THR

title: Oklahoma Athletic Director Roger Denny Slams Ground Stop Delay Of Sooners-Ole Miss College Football Game: “This Decision Isn’t Fair”

While writing that the Sooners “recognize the extraordinary circumstances” that caused the massive four-hour flight shutdown yesterday and the “challenges” it created for traveling athletic teams across the country, Denny wasn’t happy – to put it mildly – with the postponement of his team’s Saturday game to Sunday. Related Stories News Ari Emanuel Blames FAA Issues On Pete Buttigieg: "You Left A Failing System In Place" News 'Real Time': Bill Maher Jokingly Attributes FAA Issues To Selma Blair “I understand that difficult decisions sometimes must be made under extraordinary circumstances,” Denny wrote in his lengthy X post after 1 a.m. ET today. “But those decisions must also consider the impact on everyone involved. Put simply, this decision isn’t fair to our athletes, our institution or to Sooner Nation.” Watch on Deadline Read the entire statement below. More than 1,000 flights today remain delayed, with more than 3,000 today canceled, according to CNN. The Sooners-Rebels game had originally been set for today, Saturday, at 4 p.m./ET but was rescheduled last night for Sunday at 1 p.m./ET. The showdown is a home game for the Sooners, taking place at the Memorial Stadium on Oklahoma’s Norman campus. The game was postponed because the Rebels could leave Mississippi Friday due to the flight shutdowns. “As soon as we learned of Ole Miss’ travel issues,” Denny writes, “we immediately began communicating with their staff and our conference leadership. We were told that Ole Miss explored every avenue to travel to Norman and play on Saturday as planned. But, unlike every other team traveling for competition tomorrow, they were unable to find a solution. “After multiple conversations with the league office,” he continued, “Commissioner (Greg) Sankey informed us of his decision to move our game to Sunday, over our strong objection. title: How ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Pulled Off the Impossible With Latest Milestone: ‘It Will Never Happen Again’
full_text: × Nov 14, 2026 6:50am PT How ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Pulled Off the Impossible With Latest Milestone: ‘It Will Never Happen Again’ By Emily Longeretta Plus Icon Emily Longeretta 90036 emilylongeretta Latest How ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Pulled Off the Impossible With Latest Milestone: ‘It Will Never Happen Again’ 45 minutes ago ‘SVU’ Star Mariska Hargitay Breaks Down Benson and Stabler’s Complicated Reunion and Her Final Choice: ‘There Are So Many Feelings’ 2 days ago Mariska Hargitay on Filming 600 Episodes of ‘Law & Order: SVU,’ Benson’s New Journey and Revisiting Her ‘Intense History’ With Stabler 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Virginia Sherwood/NBC “Some partnerships don’t end.” It’s a quote Ice-T’s Fin said during the 600th episode of “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” on Thursday night — and one that means so much more than just the partnership between Benson and Stabler. The same could be said about Mariska Hargitay and Dick Wolf. The pair have been working together since the show debuted in 1999. “People throw around the word ‘family,'” Hargitay says. But for the “SVU” cast and crew, many who have been there from the start, it’s true. “To like them, to love them… I go to work and we hug, and it’s real. It feels like you’re going to a good dinner party when you go to work on Monday.” Related Stories ‘The Remarried Empress’ Becomes Most-Viewed Local Original Premiere Ever on Disney+ and Hulu What to Watch on Disney+ in November 2026 After the 600th episode of the Universal Television series wrapped, Wolf gathered the cast and crew for an actual dinner party, including the current cast and crew, Wolf COO Peter Jankowski and Christopher Meloni. Wolf made a speech at the beginning of the night, standing to tell the group, “This has never happened, and it will never happen again.” In a time when a show hitting 100 episodes is a major accomplishment, Hargitay never saw a world in which the NBC show would reach 600. But Wolf did, she says. And it was part of the speech she gave that night to her “SVU” family. Dick Wolf and Mariska Hargitay Andrew H. Walker/Variety “It really doesn’t feel totally real, which, in a way, is exactly how it should feel, because it’s as if we all get to live in this dream of what you thought might be possible someday. You’ve shown that it’s not only possible, but it’s so much better than anyone could have imagined,” she told Wolf. “If somebody told me that there was a show that’s been on the air for 600 episodes, I would say, ‘Really?’ That’s got to be tired. It’s got to be wheezing along. Must be running on fumes, or they’re catering to some mindless audience that just keeps coming back for some unknown reason. But here we are with a show that is healthy, that’s muscular, that’s fresh, smart, honest, and just so damn important. And yes, people keep coming back, but not for some unknown reason.” She continued, “They keep coming back because you started something very special that we’ve all had the great privilege of carrying forward for all these years.” For Hargitay, she can’t help but get emotional thinking about the love and respect the group has for one another, and for the set environment they’ve all created. It’s an environment guest stars thrive in — just look at the roster of them over the last 600 episodes — and always compliment when they arrive and leave the show. “People are happy to be there. I love making a space that’s conducive to creating, and I love making a space where people feel safe enough to try, to risk, to play, and to hunker down, and know that we’re not playing around here,” she says. “This is someone’s life. This is serious, and these are important stories. I’m so grateful.” For the milestone episode, written by showrunner Michele Fazekas and directed by Brenna Malloy, jury consultant Gwen Sharpe (J. Smith-Cameron) convinces Benson to take another look at an old case that put a man in prison for a 1998 rape and murder. When Benson revisits it, she realizes that she worked the case with Stabler (Christopher Meloni). Hesitant at first — since he failed to follow up on leads that could have revealed the truth and cut Benson out of the interrogation — Stabler ultimately joins Benson to help. While they haven’t worked together in years, he’s eager to join her on a road trip to dig deeper and put the right person behind bars. Captain Renee Curry steps in, saying, “With respect, Captain, he’s not your partner anymore. You don’t need his buy-in.” Fin quickly responds, “It doesn’t matter. Some partnerships don’t end, even when they do.” The storyline stirs up complicated feelings for both Benson and Stabler, as she realizes (and tells him), “I let you shut me out… I have to live with the fact that I didn’t do the right thing because I was new, that I didn’t follow my instinct because I thought you knew better.” For the first time with him, she really uses her voice with him as she discovers how different they both are from who they used to be when they worked together. And that’s ok — because that partnership is forever. The episode came in nearly 12 minutes over time, says Hargitay. “This was a big one. We were writing and rewriting and playing, and we had to shoot some scenes before we knew exactly what a scene was going to be, so there were a lot of different ways it could go. But it’s an embarrassment of riches.” Warner Bros. title: Venice Prizewinner ‘A Day in the Life of Jo’ Explores ‘Who and What We Truly Are’ Through Emotional Journey of Ordinary, Remarkable Teenage Girl
full_text: × Nov 14, 2026 5:32am PT Venice Prizewinner ‘A Day in the Life of Jo’ Explores ‘Who and What We Truly Are’ Through Emotional Journey of Ordinary, Remarkable Teenage Girl By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest ‘Hold Onto Me’ Director Myrsini Aristidou Kicks Off Historic Oscar Campaign for Sundance Audience Award Winner: ‘I Really Feel Like We’re Underdogs’ 20 hours ago Thessaloniki Industry Awards: Georgian Road Movie ‘The Crossroad,’ North Macedonian Drama ‘They Bloom at Dawn’ Take Top Prizes 2 days ago Oliver Laxe on Overcoming His Fears, Making Films as an Act of ‘Prayer’ and Allowing His ‘Wounds’ to Drive Him to ‘Take the Leap’ 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra" (Courtesy of Thessaloniki Film Festival) Following its prize-winning premiere at the Venice Film Festival and a whirlwind tour of the fall festival circuit, “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra,” by Greek filmmaker Jacqueline Lentzou , celebrates its homecoming this week at the Thessaloniki Film Festival , where it’s competing for top honors in the festival’s main international competition. Inspired by true events, Lentzou’s sophomore feature follows the unruly, melancholic 15-year-old Jo — played by arresting newcomer Evia Andriopoulou — as she navigates the ups and downs of a typical day in a typical teenager’s life. Drifting through a series of seemingly unrelated and inconsequential events, an otherwise ordinary day is turned upside-down with the arrival of Phaedra (Anastasia Gouliamou), a bookish classmate whose warbling rendition of an old love ballad reduces Jo to tears. In an instant, her life — her drab, unremarkable day — becomes full of possibility, hurtling toward both tragedy and transformation. Related Stories Shin Min-a, Ju Ji-hoon, Lee Jong-suk and Lee Se-young Take Webtoon Juggernaut 'The Remarried Empress' to Disney+ and Hulu Disney+ Strikes Landmark Content Deal With U.K.'s Channel 4 That Streamer Says Is Among Its 'Most Significant' Globally “A Day in the Life of Jo” premiered in the Venice Film Festival’s Horizons strand, where it won the award for best director. It’s since gone on to a healthy festival run, including stops at the New York Film Festival, the BFI London Film Festival and the Busan Film Festival. 1-2 Special will release the film in North America. Speaking to Variety in Thessaloniki, Lentzou explains that the film was inspired by tragic real-life events: the 2008 killing of 15-year-old Alexandros Grigoropoulos, whose murder at the hands of Athens police sparked nationwide protests and riots — an event that marked a brutal coming of age for Lentzou’s generation and is still commemorated with massive protests every year. While “this tragic incident served as the spark for the film,” the director says, it’s ultimately little more than a stepping stone for a profound and often moving meditation on life and the mystery of what comes after. Progressing in a loose, episodic fashion — “all days, at least my days, feel fragmented and non-linear,” Lentzou notes — it’s organized around a series of mundane events, all of which lead to an explosive, audacious and formally bold conclusion. There are squabbles with Jo’s mother (Eleni Vergeti), the girl’s sole guardian since her parents’ divorce, and a visit from her dad. Other, enigmatic encounters recall the signs and symbols that came to Jo in a dream, hinting at the porous borders between sleeping and waking, between conscious and unconscious — or, Lentzou suggests, between life and whatever comes next. At its heart is what the director describes as “the film’s existential game of who and what we truly are.” The movie is carried by a startling performance from debutante Andriopoulou, who Lentzou says she discovered “after an exhausting and admittedly disappointing two-month casting session” that ultimately led to an open call. “My hopes were not very high, yet at some point Evita enters, shyly and very, very gently, and it felt like meeting a part of me,” Lentzou explains. “I sensed a wound, a small breakage despite the youth of her age, and this is what led me to choosing her: a girl with whom I could communicate deeply.” The director went on to praise Andriopoulou’s performance as being “full of pure, honest emotion,” insisting that a recent acting prize at the Euro Balkan Film Festival in Rome would be “the start of a series of accolades” for the film’s young star. Lentzou also credits DoP Grimm Vandekerckhove for his striking cinematography, which captures the complicated play of emotions across Andriopoulou’s richly expressive face and imbues even quotidian objects and gestures with poetry and meaning. “The key in the visual approach, the big question hovering over our heads, was how to depict the invisible (already a contrast in terms), how to make the subtle presence of another awareness felt through our camera work,” Lentzou says. “I cannot stress enough how much of the film’s insane success is owed to Grimm’s contribution and faith in the project.” “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra” is produced by Avion Films and Atalante Productions in co-production with Kelek Film, 4A4 Productions, ERT and Haris & Co. title: Cinephil Boards Alexandru Solomon’s Romanian Election Doc ‘Small Expectations’ – IDFA
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie European Film Awards: ‘Fatherland’ & ‘La Bola Negra’ Top Nominations – Full List Of Films & Credits Watermelon Pictures Condemns Killing Of ‘American Doctor’ Surgeon In Gaza Hospital Strike Doha Film Festival Cancels ‘Fing!’ International Premiere View All November 14, 2026 3:40am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Small Expectations microfilm, While We’re Here EXCLUSIVE: Doc sales specialist Cinephil has boarded Alexandru Solomon ’s Small Expectations ahead of its world premiere in the Frontlight sidebar of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam next week. The first-person investigation chronicles the chaotic lead-up to Romania ’s 2025 presidential election in which moderate independent Nicușor Dan faced off against far-right forces, including Trump-aligned street fighter George Simion and ultranationalist Călin Georgescu. Solomon delves into the machinery of power, disinformation, and the rapid radicalization of a society under pressure, as Russian interference allegations, institutional breakdowns, and the unleashing of fascist energy left Romania’s democracy exposed. Related Stories Documentary IDFA Artistic Director Isabel Arrate Fernandez On Festival's Competition Lineups, "Huge" Interest In Elizabeth Holmes Doc, And AI In Documentaries Acquisitions Lightdox Acquires Sales Rights To IDFA World Premiere 'The Big Boom!', Gabriel Tejedor Film With Explosive Contradictions Production is led by award-winning Romanian company microfilm , headed by Ada Solomon, current Chair of the European Film Academy Board, in co-production with Belgium’s While We’re Here (Frederik Nicolai and Annabel Verbeke). Watch on Deadline “Following the particular case of the Romanian elections, the film is talking about very serious matters but using an approach that we wanted vivid, unconventional and entertaining at the same time,” said Alexandru Solomon and Ada Solomon in a joint statement. “We are super excited to team up with Cinephil and we are confident that we have the right partners for the international journey of the film.” Alexandru Solomon is one of Romania’s top documentarians. After starting out as a cinematographer for fiction films in the 990s and collaborating with other artists on experimental works, he shifted his focus to documentaries. His feature documentaries include The Great Communist Robbery (2004), Cold Waves – War on Radio (2007), Kapitalism, Our Secret Recipe (2010), Tarzan’s Testicle (2017). His work has played at film festivals including IDFA , Karlovy Vary, IFFR Rotterdam, been nominated for European Film Awards and won several national awards at home. His most recent film, Arsenie, An Amazing Life (2023) premiered in Karlovy Vary IFF and was screened in IDFA, Valladolid and ZagrebDox, among others. Alongside making documentaries, Soloman also teaches at University of Arts – UNArte, Bucharest, and is the president of One World Romania Association in charge of the homonym film festival, the only human rights dedicated film festival in Romania. “Few directors have mapped the fault lines of contemporary Romania with the consistency, courage, and cinematic intelligence of Alexandru Solomon. We’re honored to be collaborating with him and his team to bring Small Expectations to audiences,” said Shoshi Korman and Suzanne Nodale, co-Managing Directors of Cinephil. “As so many countries are facing the same challenges and upcoming elections around the world, the film acts as a cautionary tale of the fragility of our democracies in an ever more connected world.” Further partners include the Centrul Național al Cinematografiei (CNC), Flemish public broadcaster VRT, Romanian public broadcaster TVR, and Avanpost Media. title: ‘Hen’ Review: A Resilient Chicken Flies the Coop, Over and Over, in an Unexpectedly Stirring Survival Story
full_text: × Nov 14, 2026 3:13am PT ‘Hen’ Review: A Resilient Chicken Flies the Coop, Over and Over, in an Unexpectedly Stirring Survival Story Like 'Au Hasard Balthasar' for the humblest of barnyard animals, Hungarian director György Pálfi's film is a remarkable technical and logistical feat, but so emotionally involving you almost forget to notice. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Hen’ Review: A Resilient Chicken Flies the Coop, Over and Over, in an Unexpectedly Stirring Survival Story 4 hours ago ‘Prima Facie’ Review: Cynthia Erivo Brings Conviction, but Not Necessarily a Conviction, to an Impassioned but Clunky Legal Drama 1 day ago ‘Heartland’ Review: Jessica Chastain Rocks a Stetson and a Swagger for a Soapy Nashville Noir 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of TIFF Why did the chicken cross the road? In “ Hen ,” the answer is, as ever, to get to the other side. But the stakes are a little higher and more urgent than that in György Pálfi unassuming marvel of a creature feature: When its gallinaceous protagonist is forced across a busy highway, it’s because a hungry fox is very much on her tailfeathers. That hunter and prey in this scenario are both played by real live animals is a large part what makes “Hen” riveting: Made without CGI, with a predominantly non-human ensemble that includes eight fowl playing the lead role alone, it’s a sustained cinematic feat of fauna-wrangling unlike any other. But it’s not the miraculous novelty of the production that crosses your mind as you’re watching: In the moment, your heart pounds for that poor, dumb but surprisingly resourceful chicken, and you lock completely into her simultaneously small and vast survival saga. Related Stories Disney+ and ‘The House of Flowers’ Director Manolo Caro Prep Series Adaptation of ‘Blood Wedding’ by Federico García Lorca (EXCLUSIVE) The Game Awards Adds Disney+ to Livestream Lineup Coming from most filmmakers, “Hen” — which premiered in Toronto’s Platform competition last year, earning an honorable mention from the jury — would count as an eccentric project. But from Hungarian auteur Pálfi, whose consistently experimental oeuvre includes 2006’s Cannes-selected, shape-shifting body horror “Taxidermia” and 2018’s labyrinthine mixed-media Stanislaw Lem adaptation “His Master’s Voice,” this may be the most narratively conventional film he’s ever assembled: a grandly linear hero’s journey in which the hero just happens to be a resplendently scarlet-combed and treacle-plumed chicken, whose antagonists along the way run the gamut from wild predators to human traffickers. No life form is given precedence over another, as “Hen” limns a tense dog-eat-dog-eat-bird ecosystem — the world we all know and struggle through, just from a different vantage point. The hen in question remains nameless and voiceless from beginning to end — though the birds playing her all get star billing by name in the closing credits. (Eszti, Szandi, Feri, Enci, Eti, Enikő, Nóra and Anett, to give them their due.) Pálfi has little interest in directly anthropomorphic storytelling, and while his film is a rather eventfully scripted fiction, it aims for documentary-style naturalism and spontaneity. The obvious recent comparison point is Jerzy Skolimowski’s Oscar-nominated donkey odyssey “EO,” minus that film’s more expressionistic flourishes; Robert Bresson’s “Au Hasard Balthasar,” too, minus at least some of its despairing tragedy. It begins in a cramped industrial farm somewhere in rural Greece, where the hen’s life begins with a startlingly graphic egg-laying scene. (If you’ve ever wondered what a chicken’s cloaca looks like up close, Pálfi has you covered.) After the fledgling chick cracks her way into the outside world — standing out from the vast crowd with her uniformly dark plumage — she soon learns the cruel ways of commercial poultry-rearing and, in time, seeks a different destiny. A heart-in-mouth chain of circumstances enables her escape; via a serious of perilous scrapes, she eventually winds up at a coastal smallholding, owned by a family who get by running a shabby café on the premises, alongside other, less legal activities. There, she finds herself trapped again in the owners’ chicken coop, and put to work laying eggs: a less grim fate than the one that awaited her in the farm where she was born, perhaps, but an unhappy one just the same. Though Pálfi lightens matters with some droll music cues — the coop’s resident rooster is introduced to the grandiose strains of a romantic ballad by Greek favorite Grigoris Mpithikotsis — the film doesn’t shy from the traumatizing impact of what effectively amounts, for our feathered heroine, to recurring sexual assault, and the repeated theft of her eggs. And so she escapes, thrillingly, and more than once — motivated, it seems, by little more than some unknowing, unspoken sense that there has to be something else out there for her. In a particularly dark stab of irony, a key chance at liberation comes via her owners’ reckless venture into the trafficking of refugees. Though “Hen” maintains a sly comic sensibility throughout, there’s solemn substance to how it shows the interconnected abuse of human and animal rights alike, adding up to a portrait of a world sliding off its moral axis. That deft command and calibration of tone is as remarkable as the film’s seamless technical fluency, with every below-the-line contribution vital in cleaving to the chicken’s perspective. Vividly detailed sound design keeps us in her tiny headspace; ditto Giorgos Karvelas’ lithe, nimble cinematography, fully alert to her rhythm of movement and occasional, unpredictable moments of flighty rebellion. Editor Lehmhényi Réka, meanwhile, achieves the extraordinary feat of forging one coherent and characterful performance from footage of multiple birds — a patchworked star turn that invites and earns our complete emotional investment. A madly impractical and richly felt vision that pretty much required Pálfi to put all his eggs in one basket, “Hen” is a risk that pays off in heartening style. ‘Hen’ Review: A Resilient Chicken Flies the Coop, Over and Over, in an Unexpectedly Stirring Survival Story Reviewed online, Nov. 5, 2026. title: Spain’s FICX Gijón Festival Bets Big on International, Regional and Local Talent
full_text: × Nov 14, 2026 3:03am PT Spain’s FICX Gijón Festival Bets Big on International, Regional and Local Talent By Pablo Sandoval Plus Icon Pablo Sandoval Latest Gijón Film Festival Gives Major Awards to Ben Whishaw, Argentina’s Lisandro Alonso and Cuba’s David Bim 12 months ago Opening With Ethan Hawke’s ‘Blue Moon,’ Spain’s Gijón Festival Delivers Its Hallmark Mix of International and Spanish Emerging Talent 12 months ago Spain’s Alberto Rodriguez Opens Up on Marché du Film Standout ‘Los Tigres’ 2 years ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'I Play Rocky' closes the Gijón Film Festival. (Courtesy of Amazon/MGM) GIJÓN, Spain — Taking place in northern Spain under two monhs after the San Sebastián International Film Festival and linked to it by the Cross Roads initiative, the 64th Gijón International Film Festival (FICX) lineup stacks many of the year’s most talked-about features from international festivals such as Cannes, Berlin, Venice and Sundance. At the same time, running Nov. 13-20, the festival serves as a springboard for new local talent into the international arena, which the festival has championed for decades. Related Stories AI Audio Startup ElevenLabs Expands Nvidia Collaboration Amid CEO Jensen Huang's Affair Scandal FICX’s influence extends to the new Spanish talent currently rising with recognition: Oliver Laxe (“Sirât”), Jonás Trueba (“The Other Way Around”) and Carla Simon (“Alcarràs”) are closely linked with Gijón. Both Laxe and Trueba showcased their first works at the festival and have built long careers since their early FICX selections. Simón had her very own first retrospective at Gijón. The Gijón Festival has a long standing tradition of mixing rising and established talent, top-tier international and regional voice rubbing shoulders, becoming a beacon for emerging talent. This year’s edition opened Nov. 13 with James Gray’s “ Paper Tiger ,” screening in Gijón’s main Albar section. Gray’s previous feature, “Armageddon Time,” also opened the 2022 Gijón festival. Closing the festival on Nov. 20 is Peter Farrelly’s “ I Play Rocky ,” described by Variety’s Owen Gleiberman as “a cleverly crafted crowd-pleaser, all designed to tap into the love of ‘Rocky’ that has never gone away.” “On one side we bring big names from the international industry, as we’ve done in previous editions,” explained FICX director Alejandro Díaz Castaño. “We also bring top-Spanish talent and well-established filmmakers such as Albert Serra (“Sixteen Moments of My Life”) or Hal Hartley (“Where To Land”). Albar, the festival’s main competition, includes 21 features aiming for the top prize. Albar’s selection includes Cannes Directors’ Fortnight winner Clio Barnard’s “I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning,” Grant Lee’s Berlin Silver Bear winner “Everybody Digs Bill Evans” and Visar Morina’s “Shame and Money,” winner of the World Cinema Dramatic Grand Jury prize at Sundance. “I think we ended up having many unclassifiable features, which do not fully fit into more structured selections because of their strong auteurist component,” explained Díaz Castaño. “Here at Gijón, we are really into that mix of genres, those hybrids that tend to live on the margins.” Among the Albar titles is Valeska Grisebach’s Cannes Jury Prize winner “The Dreamed Adventure.” No stranger to either the city or the festival, Grisebach’s previous work “Longing” took the festival’s best feature prize back in 2006. Hong Sang-soo, a Gijón favorite who has won FICX best feature prize three times, arrives at this edition’s Albar with “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes,” which scooped the best director prize at Locarno. Radu Jude, another Gijón’s regular who scored Albar’s top prize in 2023 with “Do Not Expect Too Much From the End of the World,” returns with “The Diary of a Chambermaid,” which premiered at Cannes Directors’ Fortnight. “We are also lucky to have some regular, highly talented attendees from both the local and international landscape, such as Lisandro Alonso (“Eureka”), Albert Serra, Radu Jude and Hong Sangsoo,” added Díaz Castaño. László Nemes’ “Moulin,” Jeanne Herry’s “Garance” and Angela Schanelec’s “My Wife Cries” round out a competition that includes Mads Mengel’s Karlovy Vary winner “The Guest.” Nicolas Pariser’s Venice contender “One Minute to Midnight” will screen out of competition. “The Italian coda is sweet, allowing Pariser to redeem the concept of love from the cynicism of a world wary of romance,” wrote Variety’s Jay Weissberg . Retueyos, focusing on directors promoting their second or third feature, opens with Pierre Le Gall’s “Flesh and Fuel,” winner of Cannes’ Queer Palme Révélation prize. It also includes Venice Orizzonti winner Ann Sirot and Raphaël Balboni’s “Un détour par Diane.” The festival’s Premiere section brings international features to Spain for their premieres. It has expanded to 16 titles. Among attending filmmakers is Gregg Araki , who returns to the festival with Sundance title “ I Want Your Sex ,” starring Cooper Hoffman and Olivia Wilde. Araki first visited Gijón in 1996, presenting three of his early works, “The Living End,” “Totally F***ed Up” and “The Doom Generation.” He was also the subject of a 1999 FICX retrospective. Other Spain premieres take in Céline Sciamma’s cinematic essay “Tutti Frutti”; Jia Zhangke’s Cannes title “Torino Shadow”; Cédric Kahn’s Venice screener “A Place to Heal”; Ulrike Ottinger’s vampire fantasy “The Blood Countess,” starring Isabelle Huppert; and Mohammad Rasoulof’s 39-minute “Sense of Water.” Sangsoo will also be on hand for Gijón presentation of “The Day She Returns,” which is set to open in U.S. theaters next month. Thanks to the festival’s relation with its audience, its success on ticket sales and its relentless pursuit of partners and collaborations, five San Sebastián Festival titles arrive at Gijón as part of the festival’s Cross Roads initiative. The list includes Fred Cavayé’s “Les Mirsérables,” Jesse Steinberg’s “The Debut” and Javier Ruiz Caldera’s “5 More Minutes.” Gijón continues to support talent, collaborating with the Asturias Paraiso Natural Film Commision on FICX Pro, its industry wing and on the Semilleru project development lab, which provide opportunities for local Asturian and Spanish professionals. “What we aim to do is to bring the city together and push together and rally support behind the festival, working hard with local and regional entities, local government, and private initiatives and citizens. The festival becomes like a hub where everyone tunes in to connect and where everyone can find their place,” added Diaz Castaño. title: ‘Fatherland,’ ‘La Bola Negra,’ ‘Fjord’ Lead European Film Award Nominations

Both Fatherland and La Bola Negra picked up EFA noms in the best European film, European director, European screenwriter and European cinematographer categories, with Fatherland also receiving European actress and European actor noms for leads Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller for their performances, respectively, as Nobel Prize-winning writer Thomas Mann and daughter Erika. Related Stories Movies Modern Fairy Tale 'Mo Amor' Explores Identity, Transformation and Love in All Its Forms Movies 5 Takeaways From China's Golden Rooster and Hundred Flowers Film Festival Hüller received a second best European actress nom, for her starring role as a 17th-century woman masquerading as a man in Markus Schleinzer’s Rose . She’s going up against Penélope Cruz , nominated for Florian Zeller’s Bunker ; Léa Seydoux for her leading role in Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster ; Mathilde Arcel for her performance in May el-Toukhy’s Venice Festival winner Woman Unknown ; and Renate Reinsve for her starring role in Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or-winning Fjord . title: European Film Awards: ‘Fatherland’ & ‘La Bola Negra’ Top Nominations – Full List Of Films & Credits
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie European Film Awards: ‘Fatherland’ & ‘La Bola Negra’ Top Nominations – Full List Of Films & Credits Watermelon Pictures Condemns Killing Of ‘American Doctor’ Surgeon In Gaza Hospital Strike Doha Film Festival Cancels ‘Fing!’ International Premiere View All November 14, 2026 2:28am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Fatherland, La Bola Negra, Fjord Agata Grzybowska, Carla Oset/Netflix © 2026, Neon The European Film Academy has unveiled the nominations in the 16 key categories of its 39th European Film Awards taking place in Greece in January 2027. Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland leads the nominations, making it into 11 categories, followed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s La Bola Negra with ten nominations and Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes Palme d’Or winner Fjord with five. The nominations were announced in front of a live audience on Saturday at the Pavlos Zannas Theatre in the iconic Olympian building in Thessaloniki, as part of the Thessaloniki International Film Festival. Related Stories News London Film Festival: 'La Bola Negra' Wins Audience Award News 'La Bola Negra' Caliente At Box Office With $43M Worldwide, Becomes Spain's Top-Grossing Local Pic Of 2026 The winners will be unveiled at an awards ceremony on January 16 at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens, Greece, co-organised by the European Film Academy and the Ηellenic Film and Audiovisual Center. Watch on Deadline The nominations are based on the votes of 5,700 members of the European Film Academy who have been watching the films included in the annual European Film Awards Shortlis t, and will now vote for the winners. Pawlikowski’s first film in eight years , Cold War drama Fatherland stars Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller as writer Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika as they travel across Germany in 1949 from Frankfurt in West Germany to Weimar, East Germany. The Polish filmmaker shared the Cannes Best Director prize in May with Calvo and Ambrossi, whose La Bola Negra is one of the frontrunners across the award season this year. Revolving around the interconnected stories of three gay men in 1932, 1937 and 2017 , La Bola Negra has been raking in audience awards and storming the box office at home and internationally since its Cannes world premiere and Best Director win. Mungiu’s Fjord , starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve as a Romanian and Norwegian couple whose plans for a new life in a fjord village come up against neighbors with a very different outlook on life, won the director his second Cannes Palme d’Or this year, after 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days in 2007. Fifteen films have garnered a nomination in the European Film category spanning fiction, documentary and animation. Previous recent winners in the category have included Best International Feature Film Oscar winners Another Round and Sentimental Value as well as Quo Vadis, Aida? , Triangle of Sadness and Anatomy of a Fall, which won the Best Original Screenplay Academy Award. A number of documentaries have been nominated for Best Documentary and Best film including bombshell exposé NAZA , French box office break out Whispers in the Woods and Letters from A Silenced Country . Best Animation nominees also making it into the Best Film category include festival breakouts In Waves , Iron Boy and Jim Queen . The upcoming ceremony in Greece will be the second time the European Film Awards take place in a new January slot as part of a strategy to place them at the heart of the wider awards season, having taken place in December for many years. The January 16, 2027 slot once again falls the day after the end of nomination voting in the Academy Awards on January 15, and before the January 21 nominations announcement. This gives European talents in the running for the Oscars time to return home to Europe for the awards. The Golden Globes will also be done and dusted with its 2027 ceremony set for January 10. title: Modern Fairy Tale ‘Mo Amor’ Explores Identity, Transformation and Love in All Its Forms
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All November 13, 2026 10:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source ‘Mo Amor’ Courtesy of PÖFF Once upon a time… Princess Niina lived in her castle. She was courted by three suitors: The Mentor, The Writer and The Stonemason. This is, more or less, how the film Mo Amor , a tender, modern and very timely Estonian fairy tale about love in all its forms and identity, begins. And it is about to get its world premiere at the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival ( PÖFF ). Writer-director Eeva Mägi ( Mo Mamma , Mo Papa , The Weight of All the Beauty ) and her creative collaborators present a cinematic story told by a photographer named Kaur. “Princess Niina is adored by three suitors, yet remains restless, searching for something she cannot quite name,” teases a synopsis on the PÖFF website. “Then she sheds her crown and reveals her true self. Inviting her former lovers to a secluded summer home, the stage is set for a strange reunion where memory, myth, and reality begin to intertwine, old wounds resurface, and love takes unexpected forms.” Related Stories Movies 5 Takeaways From China's Golden Rooster and Hundred Flowers Film Festival Movies Joel Kinnaman to Star in Creature Thriller 'The Cell' for 'Sleeping Dogs' Director Adam Cooper (Exclusive) Mo Amor gets its world premiere on Monday, Nov. 16, in the Critics’ Picks Competition of the festival. Mägi’s previous film, Mo Papa , opened Tallinn’s Critics’ Picks section last year and earned a special mention . Mägi wrote and directed the film and produced it with Sten-Johan Lill, who also handled the cinematography. The editor was Jette Keedus. The cast features Mo Papa stars Ester Kuntu and Jarmo Reha, one of this year’s 10 rising stars in Tallinn’s Black Nights Stars showcase, as well as Tambet Tuisk, Andres Mähar, Sander Roosimägi and Ivor Mikker. Watch a trailer for Mo Amor here. Ahead of the film’s Tallinn world premiere, Mägi talked to THR about the inspiration for the film, how identity is used in political rhetoric and the lyrical quality of Mo Amor . “I always have personal stories intertwined with stories that I want to tell for society or that society needs to be told,” the filmmaker shares about her inspiration for the new movie. “I had this idea about what if love actually survives the truth, since we lie so much to people we love just to pretend we’re someone else or are sometimes so afraid to reveal who we are. But then also, transgender people are facing so many obstacles, at least in Estonia, and society is still very prejudicial towards them. So I wanted to tell a universal love story, make a transgender person a hero and show a trans man’s fairy tale.” However, Mägi also emphasizes: “Of course, there is no such thing as transgender love and ordinary love. It is all just pure love.” The idea to tell the journey of self-discovery and transformation that Niina goes on came organically in the filmmaking process. “I thought it would be even more powerful if I told it as a fairy tale because fairy tales allow us to talk about very difficult topics in very beautiful and universal ways,” she tells THR . “And it also shows that everything is possible.” ’Mo Amor’ I had the feeling that it had to be a fairy tale because this story in our society is still being seen as a fairy tale – people don’t think it’s realistic. But I think we have to tell these fairy tales until they become part of our real life.” Mägi loves bringing back collaborators from her past films because she shoots with a small budget and a very open process without a pre-written script that allows the creative team to explore the characters and storylines and see where the discovery process takes them. “I’ve been working with the same actors and actresses for years now,” she explains. “Both Jarmo Reha, who is Kaur, and Ester Kuntu, who’s playing Niina, were also in Mo Papa . Tambet Tuisk, who’s playing The Writer, was in two of my previous short films, and he’s also part of Mo Hunt , which is my next feature film – and Jarmo is there again, too. So, these actors and others [on the production] are already used to my method. We are all surfing on the same wave of chaos.” Mikker is not a professional actor, so how did he end up in Mo Amor ? “I met him at a bar,” the writer-director shares. “He’s my friend. He’s studying sculpture at the Estonian Arts Academy.” Was there an option to cast a trans actor for the film? “We couldn’t find a transgender actor to play in the film because we don’t have any [in Estonia],” the writer-director explains. “So, I talked to the trans community, and they thought that it was okay if Ester, as a woman, is playing Niina and Jarmo, as a man, is playing Kaur. And we are not so much concentrating on the transition period.” ‘Mo Amor’ That was also by choice. “We didn’t want to concentrate on the transitioning period and use a lot of makeup and do all these stereotypical things that a lot of films do,” Mägi tells THR . What Mo Amor does feature, though, is recurring photo camera sounds followed by still frames before the “action” or moving images continue. “The process itself is always guiding us,” the filmmaker emphasizes. “And when we started shooting, I realized that I wanted to have these still frames because Niina/Kaur is a photographer. I wanted to somehow make the film reflect this profession and use it as part of the cinematic storytelling.” Mo Amor was shot over the course of 17 days at the filmmaker’s boathouse on Vilsandi Island in the Baltic Sea, Estonia’s westernmost populated island. “This place is amazing,” the creative says about the island. “It’s very cinematic. And as we didn’t have any budget, as always, I decided to basically shoot it at home.” What can she share about her next feature, the briefly mentioned Mo Hunt ? “We are in post- production at the moment,” she says. And just like Mo Papa and Mo Amor are very different in terms of look, feel and atmosphere, Mo Hunt will also be a different kind of experience. “The visual language is different,” Mägi tells THR . “It’s a hybrid film, a staged documentary. I don’t want to repeat myself. And it’s also the outcome of the fact that we don’t have everything planned. We really go into the process and let the story guide us. And I guess every story has its unique ways of being reflected.” Eeva Mägi The original idea for Mo Hunt was to tell the story of a ballerina who becomes an illegal surrogate. “We started staging this ballerina, and then I had a feeling that I had to collect stories from different artists about how they have experienced the thin line between artistic creation and manipulation,” the director recalls. “Artistic creation can become exploitation or mental abuse. I was wondering how far I can push actors just for the sake of art. I understood that there are boundaries, there are limits. So, then I started to get interested in this topic and started collecting different stories from different artists.” That is why Mo Hunt will be “a staged documentary.” Explains Mägi: “All the people in the film are playing actors, but they are presenting the stories of different artists. So, the film combines what’s happening in the fiction film with what’s actually happening in artists’ hearts and minds.” THR

title: The ‘Heat’ Is On! Michael Mann & New Regency Clash In Ownership Battle Over Al Pacino & Robert De Niro 1995 Crime Classic
full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Nationwide FAA Ground Stop Lifted; Radar “Instability,” Old System Was Root Of Airspace Shutdown, Transportation Secretary Insists Microsoft “Deeply Sorry” About Global Outlook Outage, Insists Disruption Caused By “Network Capacity Upgrade” Skydance Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz Spotlights “Moral Responsibility” And Combating Antisemitism & Injustice In Simon Wiesenthal Gala Speech View All November 13, 2026 9:56pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Mann Getty Images Michael Mann won’t start filming Heat 2 until early next year, but things are already heating up legally between the acclaimed director and New Regency when it comes to 1995 crime classic. After several attempts this year by the director to reclaim ownership of the original Heat screenplay under copyright termination, the Yariv Milchan-run company today took Mann to federal court to get the trio of notices declared “defective and invalid.” In the dispute, New Regency are claiming that Mann’s role in writing the Heat screenplay was that of a “work for hire,” and therefore his termination notices are DOA. Michael Mann, Al Pacino and Robert De Niro on set of ‘Heat’ Warner Bros “We will vigorously defend this action and are confident that the courts will vindicate Michael Mann’s statutory rights under the Copyright Act,” Mann’s team says. “For clarification, this is unrelated to production of Heat 2 which will begin shooting on January 19.” In that context, the 1991 founded New Regency is thinking of the past and the future, the company’s Kendall Brill & Kellyl awyers say. “If given effect, the Termination Notices would purport to strip Regency, beginning in 2028, of rights it has held for more than three decades, clouding Regency’s title to the Screenplay and jeopardizing its ability to develop, finance, and license works derived from it,” the 20-page complaint for declaratory relief states. “In addition, certain provisions of the agreements that Mann and Regency each entered into with Amazon with respect to Heat 2 depend on the outcome of this litigation.” Speaking of the much anticipated, Heat 2 , the Leonardo DiCaprio, Christian Bale , Adam Driver, Stephen Graham and Jason Clarke starrer will see Mann directing the prequel flick from his own script. This particular script is based on Mann and Meg Gardiner’s No. 1 New York Times bestselling novel from 2022. title: ‘Cookie Queens’ Director Says Girl Scout Cookies Were “A Delicious Way In” to a Larger Conversation (Video)
full_text: Skip to main content By Scott Feinberg Plus Icon Scott Feinberg Executive Editor of Awards ScottFeinberg Follow Sign Up View All November 13, 2026 9:36pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Alysa Nahmias during a 'Cookie Queens' Q&A at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival Jason Kempin/Getty Images for SCAD In a year packed with oppressively heavy and disspiriting documentaries, a breath of fresh air is Cookie Queens , Alysa Nahmias ’ chronicle of four young girls’ efforts, in the face of varying forms of adversity, to meet their goals during Girl Scouts cookie-selling season. The film premiered at Sundance, won the audience award at SXSW and has become the year’s highest-grossing non-celebrity doc. In late October, Nahmias brought the film to the SCAD Savannah Film Festival , where it screened in the fest’s celebrated Docs to Watch sidebar — followed by a Q&A that you can watch below — and during which she was also one 10 directors of outstanding 2026 docs who appeared on the fest’s Doc to Watch Panel , moderated by yours truly. Related Stories Movies How the Oscar-Winning Directors of 'Free Solo' Confronted Tragedy -- And Their Own Filmmaking -- in 'Everest: The Other Side' Movies 'One in a Million' Filmmaker on the Ethical Dilemma He Faced and Learning to Let His Subject Find Her Own Way Nahmias has been directing and producing docs for the past 20 years. Her focus had long been on art and architecture, but her young kids nudged her to make something that they and their friends could enjoy. When a friend recounted to her his experience of being complimented by a young girl who then then hit him up to buy some of her Girl Scout cookies, she was pretty sure that she found just such a project. Nahmias, who was never a Girl Scout herself (her mother was a Brownie), felt that chronicling the journeys of several Girl Scouts over the course of one cookie-selling season could be a vehicle to explore girlhood, why women of all ages are underestimated, and more. “I wasn’t actually that interested in the cookies,” she explains. “The Girl Scouts of it all was wonderful and a way in — a delicious way in. But it was sort of honey on the razor’s edge of thinking about what it means to be a girl in American capitalism.” Nahmias met with Girl Scouts of the USA, but ultimately decided to make a film independent of the nation youth organization that oversees Girl Scouts (and, incidentally, was founded back in 1912 in, of all places, Savannah, Georgia). She set out to “cast” her film with girls representing a diversity of racial and ethnic demographics, economic backgrounds, and geography, ultimately finding seven whose families would consent to her filming them over the course of a six-month stretch, during which Nahmias and her team constantly traversed the country chronicling them. Stylistically, Nahmias was as inspired by scripted projects about childhood, such as The Florida Project , Moonrise Kingdom and Petit Maman , as she was by documentaries, like Salesman , Spellbound and Boys State . One big takeaway: she always shot from the kids’ POVs. In the end, Nahmias decided to cut out the stories of three girls and focus the film on four: Olive, a smooth-talking go-getter who has something of a tiger mom; Nikki, who dreams of being as cool as her older sisters; Shannon Elizabeth, the sweet child of a financially-strapped couple; and Ara, a diabetic with a bright-eyed view of the world. Some might assume that the film is a competition doc in which the girls ultimately cross paths, but in fact, they never met until after the film was locked. “I was never interested in how many boxes the girls sold,” Nahmias emphasizes. “I was always interested in their inner journeys.” THR

title: Ari Emanuel Blames FAA Issues On Pete Buttigieg: “You Left A Failing System In Place”

title: Michael Mann Seeks to Reclaim Rights to Original ‘Heat’ Screenplay
full_text: × Nov 13, 2026 6:51pm PT Michael Mann Seeks to Reclaim Rights to Original ‘Heat’ Screenplay By Gene Maddaus Plus Icon Gene Maddaus Senior Media Writer @GeneMaddaus Latest Michael Mann Seeks to Reclaim Rights to Original ‘Heat’ Screenplay 13 hours ago Amid Flight Halt, Trump Meets With Jon Voight to Talk U.S. Film Incentive: ‘Get This Done!’ 16 hours ago Judge Refuses to Dismiss Trump’s $10 Billion Defamation Suit Against BBC 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images Michael Mann , who is set to begin shooting the long-awaited “ Heat 2 ” in January, is in a legal dispute with New Regency as he seeks to reclaim the copyright to his screenplay for the original film. New Regency produced “Heat,” released in 1995. The company filed a lawsuit on Friday arguing that it still owns the copyright to the original screenplay. Earlier this year, Mann’s lawyers sent termination notices invoking the right to reclaim the copyright. New Regency argues that the screenplay was a “work made for hire,” and is thus ineligible for copyright termination. Related Stories The Game Awards Adds Disney+ to Livestream Lineup What to Watch on Disney+ in November 2026 New Regency argues that Mann’s termination action clouds its ownership of the original “Heat,” and is seeking a declaration that the termination notices are void. Mann’s lawyers intend to fight the lawsuit “vigorously,” his reps said in a statement. “We will vigorously defend this action and are confident that the courts will vindicate Michael Mann’s statutory rights under the Copyright Act,” a spokesperson said. “This filing has to do with original and personal writing Michael Mann did on multiple screenplays during the 1980s and which evolved into the iconic 1995 film ‘Heat’ that Mann wrote, produced and directed. After 40 years Michael Mann is exercising the right of authors to reclaim their work and in this case Michael Mann’s original creation.” Mann developed the characters and the story that would become “Heat” over two decades, beginning in the 1970s. According to the lawsuit, Warner Bros. acquired the rights to the “Heat” screenplay in 1994 in a deal with Mann’s loan-out company. The suit alleges that deal was explicitly a “work made for hire” agreement — not an assignment of rights — and that therefore it cannot be terminated. Authors are allowed to terminate assignments of rights after 35 years under the Copyright Act. According to the suit, Mann’s lawyers initially told New Regency that Mann had assigned his rights to his loan-out companies in 1988, and was thus seeking to terminate that agreement. New Regency sought a copy of that agreement, and was told it was an oral agreement, the suit states. “The Oral Assignment on which the First Termination Notice is based supposedly derives from an oral agreement that Mann allegedly made with himself, in which Mann, like a Shakespearean actor playing multiple parts, simultaneously spoke on his own individual behalf, as well as on behalf of MMCo. and ZZY,” the lawsuit states. Two subsequent termination notices were submitted cited other agreements, both of which New Regency claims are also invalid. Warner Bros. was originally set to produce “Heat 2,” but backed out of the project last year. Amazon MGM Studios has since acquired the film. Both Mann and New Regency have done deals with Amazon that account for the copyright dispute, with Mann assigning any rights he may reclaim to Amazon, according to the complaint. In other words, however the dispute comes out, “Heat 2” should be unaffected. “For clarification, this is unrelated to production of Heat 2 which will begin shooting on January 19,” Mann’s rep said in a statement. ‘Harry Potter’ HBO Series Casts Its Arthur Weasley, Moaning Myrtle, Colin Creevey ‘Harry Potter: A Forbidden Forest Experience’ Returns to New York Just in Time for Halloween — Here’s How to Get Tickets ‘Harry Potter’ Star Paapa Essiedu Says ‘I Don’t Want to Talk About’ J.K. title: DC Studios To-Do List: Here’s What Incoming Boss Jeremy Latcham Will Sort Through From The Gunn-Safran Era
full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony DC Studios To-Do List: Here’s What Incoming Boss Jeremy Latcham Will Sort Through From The Gunn-Safran Era Isla Fisher & Blake Ritson Join Al Pacino In John Paul Getty III Kidnapping Pic ‘Captivated’ Johnny Depp Pic ‘Ebenezer’ Opening To Spirited $20M+ U.S. – Box Office Update View All November 13, 2026 6:45pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Clockwise from top left: 'Superman,' Skyler Gisondo in 'Superman,' Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler in 'Lanterns' and 'Robert Pattinson in 'The Batman II' Warner Bros Pictures/DC/Everett Collection The news earlier this week of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s exit from DC shook the town like Suicide Squad ‘s Starro stomping down Melrose Avenue. Now it’s up to incoming former Marvel executive and Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves producer Jeremy Latcham to sort through the groundwork that was laid before by the duo. You can check out the list of lingering and active DC projects below. Note, Latcham starts the job December 1, and we understand that no mandates have been given to him by Skydance co-CEO David Ellison in regards to what’s prioritized among those projects in development. Related Stories Executives Departing DC Co-Head James Gunn Reflects On “Trying” Four Years, Juggling Being Filmmaker & Exec News The 65 Movies That Have Made More Than $1 Billion At The Global Box Office Gunn and Safran’s “Gods and Monsters” vision, which was first unveiled in January 2023 , was realized at 40%, with movies Superman and Supergirl made along with TV series Lanterns and Creature Commandos. Having seen the ills in the Marvel Cinematic Universe owing to its overindulgence in the Disney+ era with features being fast-tracked and storylines between series and movies mish-moshed, Gunn was adamant about not rushing projects through development — or worse, going into production on a movie that was missing a third act. If a project wasn’t ready, it wasn’t ready, which is why we saw some of the early pitches promised — i.e., Paradise Lost and Booster Gold series, and the antihero team The Authority feature — ultimately stall. Watch on Deadline James Mangold was circling Swamp Thing at one point a few years ago, but the five-time Oscar-nominated filmmaker is currently making his Paramount+ series Copland a priority. Not to mention he’s also working on a motocross heist screenplay that reteams him with his A Complete Unknown star Timothée Chalamet for the film studio. Another thing Gunn and Safran wanted to correct in Warners’ DC-verse were the dueling TV and film mythologies for superheroes. Quite often a superhero’s storyline on TV was different on the big screen, or worse, competed against each other. Case in point: the CW series of Flash ended in May 2023, three weeks before the Ezra Miller-fronted movie hit theaters and bombed with $271.4 million worldwide off a $200M production cost before P&A (the star’s tabloid headlines at the time didn’t help the movie either). The Gunn and Safran DC universe would see their characters having direct lines through live-action film and TV. Above all, Gunn’s m.o. was to bring zhuzh to a franchise that had grown stale after Christopher Nolan’s Dark Knight series. It will be interesting to see whether Latcham remains as strict as Gunn and Safran were on development. L-R: Jeremy Latcham and James Gunn at an event for Marvel’s ‘Avengers: Age of Ultron’ in 2015 Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images for Disney) In the run-up to the Paramount-Warner Bros merger, Gunn and Safran didn’t greenlight any live-action feature films beyond what was currently in production, so only The Batman Part II , Man of Tomorrow and The Dynamic Duo. Gunn has teased he’s got a screenplay he’s penning in the DC-verse post- Man of Tomorrow, but that greenlight will be up to Team Latcham (he worked with Gunn during Guardians of the Galaxy ). A bulk of what Gunn and Safran leave behind to DC’s new owners are animated TV series. Given the nature of animation production, many of these projects are already in the works even though many don’t have a streaming or network home, or even a renewal. The new Warner Bros under Skydance co-CEOs Ellison and Ynon Kreiz remains strictly about keeping everything in the black. In a recent earnings call, the two were vocal about the bleeding that was going on in the YTD Warner Bros feature slate. There’s no room for box office kryptonite ala this past summer’s blunder Supergirl (production cost $186M, global box office $126.4M), arguably the only big miss during the Gunn and Safran administration (versus the previous Walter Hamada-run era that yielded The Flash, Shazam: Fury of the Gods and Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom ). Above all, the new Paramount administration, which declined comment for this story, is conscious about not repeating history, meaning cancelling a near-completed project to the greater upset of the town (remember how David Zaslav swatted Batgirl in August 2022? That was all before Gunn and Safran arrived on the scene). Below is the list of projects remaining at DC. Robert Pattinson as The Batman Warner Bros. Dated or In the Pipeline Man of Tomorrow (dir. James Gunn) – The Superman sequel starring David Corenswet, Rachel Brosnahan and Nicholas Hoult is in post-production and set for release on July 9, 2027. Buzz is that Lanterns segues into this Superman. Gunn took to Threads to respond to rumors that Skydance is making edits to the film. “No one from Skydance has even seen the movie – the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. So any stories around this narrative are false,” exclaimed the MCU and DCU filmmaker. The Batman Part II (dir. Matt Reeves). Steven Soderbergh is working with The Batman II director Matt Reeves to help finish principal photography during final weeks of the sequel to 2022’s $772M-grossing Robert Pattinson movie for a February 18, 2028 theatrical release. The two will remain in communication until filming has ended with Reeves taking over post-production duties when he is ready to return. Production was paused in October as Reeves was attending a family matter. Dynamic Duo (dir Arthur Mintz) – The origin story of the Robins is a co-production with Warner Bros Pictures Animation, 6th and Idaho and New Orleans animation studio Swaybox. The latter is known for their “momo animation,” which is a cross between CGI animation, stop-motion practical elements and live-action real-time performance. Pic will hit theaters on September 22, 2028. TV Bat-Fam – Season 1 premiered in November 2025, with the second half of the season still to air on the Prime Video series showrun by Mike Roth. Batman, Alfred and young Damian Wayne — having taken on the mantle of “Little Batman” — welcome a few new residents to Wayne Manor. Joining the family dinner table is Alicia Pennyworth, Alfred’s free-spirited grandniece; Claire, a recently reformed Super-Villain; Ra’s al Ghul, Damian’s adoring “Pap Pap” who also happens to be Batman’s longtime nemesis; and Man-Bat, who takes up residence in the belfry. Oh! And let’s not forget Selina, the beloved family cat. This close-knit family of misfits navigate the fun and frustrations of ordinary life while protecting the streets of Gotham City. Batman Caped Crusader – The Prime Video series has clocked two seasons and is awaiting renewal. Executive producers/showrunners are James Tucker and Geoffrey Thorne. EPs are Bruce Timm, James Abrams and Matt Reeves. Warner Bros. Animation Batman: Knightfall – The home entertainment animated feature from director Jeff Wamester and producer Jim Krieg. Part 1 was released in August, Part 2 is happening in December and Part 3 is coming in 2027. This movie event brings to life one of the most iconic sagas in Batman comics history. The People vs Gorilla Grood – The HBO half hour comedy series, a spinoff of Gunn’s Superman, centers around Skyler Gisondo’s Jimmy Olsen and Jimmy Tatro’s titular ape. It is in post-production with no airdate yet. A super-intelligent ape is convicted of murdering his father, the King of Gorilla City. In an eight-part “true” crime docuseries, the Daily Planet ’s Olsen reopens the case, investigating whether Gorilla Grodd was wrongly convicted in one of Metropolis’ most famous murder trials. Tony Yacenda and Dan Perrault are showrunners, writers and EPs. Frankenstein and Rick Flag Sr. from ‘Creature Commandos’ Max Creature Commandos Season 2 – The James Gunn-created series is in production for a second season; Gunn previously mentioned that an airdate was being eyed for the latter part of 2027. The series follows incarcerated monsters who are recruited for missions deemed too dangerous for humans. Characters joining in Season 2 are Khalis the Mummy, King Shark and Nosferata. Dean Lorey is the showrunner and EP. DC Super Powers – In production, with a network and streaming home TBD. Matt Beans is the showrunner. At the Alliance School for Heroes, new students Lightning, Flash, Plastic Man, Aquagirl, Green Lantern and Terra level up their powers under the supervision of Principal Martian Manhunter in the hopes of one day graduating and becoming the next generation of Earth’s defenders. Get Jiro – Season 1 is currently airing on Adult Swim, while Season 2 awaits a greenlight. EPs are showrunners Jordan Blum, Alessandro Tanaka and Brian Gatewood. Starring Brian Tee ( Chicago Med ), Get Jiro transports viewers to a post-apocalyptic, near-future Los Angeles where culinary culture reigns supreme and the world’s most powerful figures are chefs. In this society where food is both currency and a demarcation of class, the mysterious sushi chef Jiro (Tee) sets out on a quest for vengeance. Joker: Laugh Riot – The anime Joker series from director Yasuhuro Aoki ( ChaO ) is in its early days of production, has been greenlit to series and will be taken to market. When Batman is murdered, the Joker launches a ruthless crusade through Gotham’s underworld to find the killer who took away his greatest adversary. But as his violent quest for answers pushes him closer towards vigilante than villain, Joker is forced to confront the truth that without Batman, he doesn’t know who he is. Mister Miracle – Tom King, who wrote the Mister Miracle comics with Mitch Gerads, is showrunning and EPing this animated series that follows the “odyssey” of Scott Free aka Mister Miracle. Announced at Annecy 2025, the blurb for this series reads: No prison can hold him. No trap can contain him. He is Scott Free, the worldwide celebrity sensation known as Mister Miracle, and he is the greatest escape artist who ever lived. But can he pull off the ultimate trick – and escape death itself? Something goes horribly wrong with the perfect life that Scott and his warrior wife Big Barda have built for themselves on Earth.” The series is in production but hasn’t been sold to a platform yet. It will be taken to market. My Adventures with Green Lantern – Jake Wyatt, who is also the EP on My Adventures with Superman , is the showrunner for the 10-episode animated series, which follows Jessica Cruz ( Moana ‘s Auliʻi Cravalho), who made her first appearance in the third season of My Adventures with Superman . She’s a student at Hal Jordan Memorial High. Things get even worse when more debris from the Lanterns’ ancient space war arrives – along with their alien foes. To protect the Earth, Jess will have to overcome her fears, anxieties and your typical teenage drama to lead a new Lantern Corp against a terrifying foe. Other Green Lantern characters in the show include Kyle Rayner and Kilowog. In production but not not sold to a platform a yet. My Adventures With Superman – This hasn’t been picked up for a fourth season but just finished Season 3 on Adult Swim. Jake Wyatt is EP/showrunner. It’s the animated version of the Superman story with Superman falling in love with Lois Lane and her taking Jimmy Olsen under her wing. Starfire – Josie Campbell, a writer on My Adventures with Superman , is leading the animated series project for DC Studios and Warner Bros. Animation. The series followed the beloved Teen Titans superhero’s origins when she discovers an ancient spacecraft on her home planet and ventures out to the deepest places of the DC universe. In production but not sold to a platform yet. Teen Titans Go! – The longest-running DC animated series, with Season 9 currently airing on Cartoon Network and approaching its 500th episode. Luke Cormican is the showrunner. Cartoon Network’s ‘Teen Titans’ Cartoon Network / Courtesy: Everett Collection In early development Film Batman: Brave and the Bold – The feature project was first announced in 2023 when Gunn and Safran unveiled their “Gods and Monsters” slate with Flash director Andy Muschietti attached to direct. Christina Hodson did a draft of the script. There’s been no movement on this for quite some time however and it’s current slate is unclear. Muschietti has been busy on Season 2 of HBO’s IT: Welcome to Derry. The comic revolves around Batman and his son, Damien Wayne, as Robin “who is a little son of a bitch,” exclaimed Gunn back in 2023. “Assassin, murderer who Batman takes on, who is Batman’s actual son that he doesn’t know exists for the first 8-10 years of his life… it’s a strange father-and-son story about the two of them and based on Grant Morrison’s run of The Batman.” The dilemma with this project from the start is that it’s a complete reboot of Batman, and with the success of Reeves’ The Batman and its upcoming sequel, it’s unclear how two Batman live-action feature franchises could ever exist. Savage Hunters – Aka the Bane and Deathstroke movie. Greg Mottola was attached to direct off a screenplay by Matthew Orton. Teen Titans – At lst report, Supergirl scribe Ana Nogueira was taking a stab at it. Wonder Woman – Ana Nogueira was also writing the first draft of this. TV Absolute Batman – From EP Scott Snyder, the series will reinvent the Batman mythos for a new generation of fans, reimagining the Dark Knight as a working-class hero up against impossible odds (and the most terrifying foes ever), on a mission to prove that even in an era of wealth, power and corruption, one good person can change the world. When you take away the manor, the money, the advantages, what you’re left with is something absolute. No network yet. Blue Beetle – Per Deadline’s first report over two years ago, Miguel Puga ( The Casagrandes ) was showrunner and director with Cristian Martinez ( Women of the Movement , Good Trouble ) set as writer of the animated series. Angel Manuel Soto and Gareth Dunnet-Alcocer, director and screenwriter of the 2023 film, respectively, were set to EP alongside John Rikard who served in the same capacity on the film. Untitled Krypto Project – From EP C.H. Greenblatt. When he’s not hanging out with Superman or Supergirl, doggie Krypto tags along with a gang of misfit criminal wannabes who live down the block, and they soon discover he’s a ball of destructive, lovable energy worse than any of them. As he follows them into misadventures and poorly laid plans, Krypto’s pure nature slowly ends up redeeming them, whether they want it or not. No network yet. Lanterns Season 2 – Chris Munday has assembled the writers room but no greenlight has been given to this HBO viewership hit. Lanterns’ Season 1 finale pulled in 10.5M global viewers in its first three days, a series high. Poison Ivy – Tw-time Emmy-nominated The Penguin showrunner Lauren LeFranc is in talks to produce. In regards to a Penguin Season 2, there is nothing in the works as Batman II is the most immediate priority.
